reconcile.connective: Gill proposes a single solution to both the count and the direction problem: two separate healing encounters at Jericho, one on the approach and one on departure, totaling three blind men in all.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the plain reading: Mark and Luke each describe a single blind man, and Luke sets the healing on Jesus's approach to Jericho rather than his departure, so no single scene fits all three texts.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/blindmen.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: but to me it seems, that there were three blind men cured; one before he went into Jericho, which Luke only relates, and two as he came out of Jericho, which Matthew here speaks of; and one of which, according to Mark, was by name Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill directly proposes his own resolution to both the count (Matthew's two vs. Mark/Luke's one) and direction (Luke's approach vs. Matthew/Mark's departure) problems: three blind men healed across two separate encounters at Jericho, one of the second pair being Bartimaeus.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact triple ("Blind men, Matt. xx. 30 and Mark x. 46; Luke xviii. 35, 38") directly, canvassing the same harmonizations found in the row's commentary notes: a three-blind-men/two-encounter reading, a two-blind-men reading with Matthew condensing the approach and departure into one scene, and reading Luke's verb as 'near' rather than 'approaching' (verified via curl+grep of the archive.org djvu full text, pp. 386-387).

link.title: Matthew 20:29-34 says Jesus healed two blind men as He left Jericho. Mark 10:46-52 and Luke 18:35-43 say He healed one man as He entered Jericho. Is this a contradiction?
link.note: argues Mark and Luke spotlight the more prominent beggar (Bartimaeus) without denying a second was present, and notes the possibility of two Jerichos (old and new) accounting for the entering/leaving difference
